monument_name: Tarpibaḍā Fountain (constructed between the 13th and 15th centuries)
description_en: The Fountain, constructed between the 13th and 15th centuries, is about some 20 meters south of twośikharatemples (JUM0441andJUM0442). The three monuments (twośikharatemples and Fountain) are built on terraces currently planted with apple trees on the eastern bank of the Sinja River, opposite the villages of Jacha (to the south-west) and Tarpibaḍā (to the north-west). D. R. Sharma describes the monuments (Sharma 2012: 192-193).The Fountain is carved into the hillside and faces west. It has a vertical stone facing carved with plinths and projections (skt.bhadra), similar to theśikharatemple facades. Two spouts in the upper section are connected to a buried supply pipe. The spouts are shaped with the head of amakara, similar to the medieval fountains (hiti) in the Kathmandu Valley. On both sides of the central panel are platforms. The water cascades between the two side platforms onto a stone slab. The front side of the Fountain is richly adorned with carvings of various decorative patterns.Fountains, known asmugrāhā, are scattered throughout the Karnali basin (Nep.dhārō), particularly in the valleys of the Kalikot and Jumla districts, so that a traveller will come across one to three during his day's walk. These types of fountains are most likely from Uttarakhand, near the monolithic temple of Ek Hatia in Almiya (Chanchani 2019: 111 and Andolfatto 2019). Their construction in Uttarakhanda dates back to the 10th century. Such water architecture seems to have appeared later in west Nepal, most likely around the 12th century. In this case, we can speculate that Tarbibaḍā Fountain is contemporaneous with the two nearbyśikharatemples (JUM0441 and JUM0442), which were probably built between the 13th and 15th centuries. This time period corresponds to the end of the Khaśa Malla kingdom (12th-14th century) and the beginning of the Kalyāl dynasty's rule from Jumla (15th century) (Andolfatto 2019).
